nodes.note: It is a developmental anomaly of the aorta itself (thickened media and an infolded ridge), not a problem of partitioning, transposition or fetal circulation.

nodes.q: By its position relative to the ductus, which type does a pink 7-year-old with rib notching have?
nodes.note: Collaterals develop over years, so rib notching appears. The preductal (infantile) type needs a patent ductus to perfuse the lower body, giving cyanosis of the legs only (differential cyanosis); it is linked to Turner syndrome.

nodes.q: Why is the pressure in his left arm lower than in his right?
nodes.a: The left subclavian artery arises at or just beyond the narrowing
nodes.note: The left arm is then downstream of the obstruction.

nodes.q: Which vessels carry the collateral flow that notches the ribs?
nodes.note: Enlarged, tortuous intercostal arteries erode the lower rib margins, usually seen after age 5 to 6.

nodes.q: Why does the electrocardiogram show large left ventricular voltages?
nodes.a: Left ventricular hypertrophy from pressure overload against the narrowed aorta
nodes.note: A pressure-loaded left ventricle hypertrophies concentrically; in newborns the right ventricle dominates.

nodes.q: Which valve abnormality coexists in more than half of patients?
nodes.note: Bicuspid aortic valve occurs in about half or more of patients. Turner syndrome (45,X) is the other classic association, mainly in girls.

nodes.q: Which brain complication does the high pressure upstream risk?
nodes.a: Rupture of a berry aneurysm causing subarachnoid hemorrhage
nodes.note: Also aortic dissection or rupture, heart failure, and infective endocarditis at the bicuspid valve.

nodes.q: What is the definitive treatment?
nodes.a: Surgical resection with end-to-end anastomosis, or balloon angioplasty with a stent in older children
nodes.note: A newborn with critical coarctation and a ductus-dependent circulation needs prostaglandin E1 to keep the ductus open until surgery. Hypertension may persist after repair.

nodes.q: A murmur below the left clavicle could suggest a patent ductus arteriosus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Continuous machinery murmur under the left clavicle + bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure**; equal arm and leg pressures
**Arm pressure higher than leg pressure + weak delayed femoral pulses**; ejection murmur, no continuous murmur

nodes.note: The trap: both murmurs sit below the left clavicle and a ductus can coexist with a preductal coarctation.

nodes.q: The cause of his defect could be offered as transposition of the great arteries. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Cyanosis from the first hours of life + egg-on-a-string heart on x-ray**; aorta from the right ventricle
**No cyanosis + arm-to-leg pressure gap**

nodes.q: The cause of his defect could be offered as persistent fetal circulation. How do you tell them apart?

split.a: Persistent fetal circulation (persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn)
split.note: **Cyanosis in the first days with right-to-left shunting across the ductus or foramen ovale**; normal arm and leg pressures
**Pink child with hypertension in the arms and weak femoral pulses**

nodes.q: His ventricular pressure overload could suggest pulmonary valve stenosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Right ventricular hypertrophy with right axis deviation; ejection click and murmur at the left upper sternal border that gets louder on inspiration**; normal leg pulses
**Left ventricular hypertrophy with left axis deviation + weak femoral pulses**

root.stem: A 4-day-old boy has a mild bluish color that worsens when he cries, fast breathing and poor feeding. He has a cleft palate and low-set ears. A single loud second heart sound and a harsh systolic murmur are heard at the left sternal border, and his pulses are bounding. The chest x-ray shows an enlarged heart with increased lung markings and no visible thymus shadow, and his blood calcium is low. There is no egg-on-a-string heart, no boot-shaped heart and no difference between arm and leg blood pressures.
root.oneliner: 4-day-old M + mild cyanosis worse with crying + tachypnea, poor feeding + cleft palate, low-set ears + single loud second heart sound + harsh systolic murmur at left sternal border + bounding pulses + cardiomegaly with increased lung markings + absent thymus shadow + low calcium + no egg-on-a-string, no boot shape, no arm-leg pressure gap
highlight: mild bluish color that worsens when he cries
no egg-on-a-string heart, no boot-shaped heart and no difference between arm and leg blood pressures

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A single arterial trunk leaves the heart and gives rise to the aorta, pulmonary arteries and coronary arteries. The clincher: **mild cyanosis with a single loud second heart sound, bounding pulses and increased lung markings, in an infant with a cleft palate, no thymus shadow and low calcium**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: All describe a failure of the outflow tract to divide.

nodes.q: Which embryologic structure fails to form?
nodes.note: This spiral septum normally divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

nodes.q: Which migrating cells are needed to form this septum?
nodes.note: If cardiac neural crest cells are missing, the septum does not form, so the truncus persists.

nodes.q: Which chromosomal deletion explains his cleft palate, absent thymus shadow and low calcium?
nodes.note: The third and fourth pharyngeal pouches and neural crest are involved: thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia, cardiac defects, abnormal face, cleft palate (CATCH-22).

nodes.q: Which defect almost always accompanies it?
nodes.note: The trunk overrides the defect and receives blood from both ventricles, so the blood mixes.

nodes.q: Why does heart failure appear in the first weeks rather than at birth?
nodes.a: Pulmonary vascular resistance falls after birth, so more blood flows to the lungs
nodes.note: A growing left-to-right shunt overloads the lungs and the left heart, so there is tachypnea, poor feeding and cardiomegaly.

nodes.q: Which complication appears years later if it is not repaired?
nodes.note: Pulmonary vascular disease raises resistance until the shunt reverses to right-to-left, with cyanosis and clubbing.

nodes.q: Which test confirms it?
nodes.note: It shows one outflow vessel overriding a ventricular septal defect.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Early surgical repair in the first weeks of life
nodes.note: Close the septal defect and connect the right ventricle to the pulmonary arteries with a conduit. Treat heart failure and give calcium for hypocalcemia while waiting.

nodes.q: Cyanosis from a septation defect could suggest transposition of the great arteries. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Severe cyanosis in the first hours + egg-on-a-string heart**; the aorticopulmonary septum fails to spiral, so the aorta arises from the right ventricle
**One arterial trunk + mild cyanosis + increased lung markings + single second sound**; the septum never forms

nodes.note: The trap: both come from abnormal aorticopulmonary septation.

nodes.q: Cyanosis in an infant could suggest tetralogy of Fallot. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Boot-shaped heart + decreased lung markings + tet spells relieved by squatting**; pulmonary stenosis causes a right-to-left shunt
**Increased lung markings + single second sound + bounding pulses**

nodes.q: A heart murmur in a baby could suggest an atrial septal defect. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fixed split second heart sound + soft systolic flow murmur**; no cyanosis in infancy, usually silent
**Single second sound + cyanosis in the first days + heart failure**

nodes.q: Bounding pulses could suggest coarctation of the aorta. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Arm blood pressure higher than leg pressure + weak delayed femoral pulses**; no cyanosis
**Equal arm and leg pressures; bounding pulses from diastolic runoff into the lungs + cyanosis**

root.stem: A 46-year-old man has fainted twice while hurrying uphill and has had several months of chest tightness on exertion. His younger brother was told at birth that he had a heart valve variant. A harsh systolic ejection murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border and radiates to the neck, preceded by an ejection click that does not change with breathing. His pulses are weak and slow to rise. Echocardiography shows a thickened, calcified aortic valve that opens in an oval, fish-mouth shape in systole and has a single closure line in diastole, and an ascending aorta of 4.4 cm. He has had no fever, blood cultures were negative, he has never had rheumatic fever, and his mitral valve is normal.
root.oneliner: 46M + two exertional faints + exertional chest tightness + brother with valve variant + harsh systolic ejection murmur at right upper sternal border radiating to neck + ejection click unchanged with breathing + weak slow-rising pulses + calcified aortic valve with fish-mouth opening and single closure line + ascending aorta 4.4 cm + no fever, negative blood cultures + no rheumatic fever, normal mitral valve
highlight: younger brother was told at birth
ejection click that does not change with breathing
pulses are weak and slow to rise
no fever, blood cultures were negative

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A congenital aortic valve with two cusps instead of three. The clincher: **an ejection click before a systolic ejection murmur + a fish-mouth opening with a single closure line on echocardiography**, with stenosis decades earlier than usual.

nodes.q: How does the valve end up with two cusps?
nodes.a: Two of the three cusps fuse, most often the right and left coronary cusps
nodes.note: A ridge (raphe) marks the fusion. It is the most common congenital heart malformation (about 1-2% of people), more frequent in men, and runs in families.

nodes.q: Which valve lesion does his abnormal valve develop decades earlier than a normal valve, from turbulent flow and calcium deposition?
nodes.note: Symptoms appear in the 40s to 60s, a decade or two earlier than in a normal tricuspid valve; angina, syncope and heart failure.

nodes.q: Why can exertion cause fainting or sudden death?
nodes.a: The fixed obstruction stops cardiac output from rising while muscle vessels dilate, so blood pressure and brain and heart perfusion fall
nodes.note: Collapse during running, as in the classic case, is often due to arrhythmia from ischemia.

nodes.q: What does the valve look like at autopsy?
nodes.a: A thickened, calcified valve with two cusps and a fused ridge
nodes.note: The opening is narrowed and fish-mouth shaped. An infected valve would show vegetations, a myxomatous valve floppy redundant leaflets, and a rheumatic valve three cusps fused at the commissures.

nodes.q: His ascending aorta measures 4.4 cm. Which aortic problem is linked to this valve?
nodes.a: Ascending aortic dilation (aneurysm) from cystic medial degeneration, with risk of dissection
nodes.note: The aortic wall defect is intrinsic and happens even if the valve works well.

nodes.q: Which other congenital aortic defect most often coexists?
nodes.note: Turner syndrome is the other classic association.

nodes.q: Which infection is he at risk of because of the abnormal valve?
nodes.note: The damaged valve surface traps bacteria after bacteremia; a viridans streptococcus after dental work is typical.

nodes.q: Who else needs screening?
nodes.note: The condition is familial.

nodes.q: What is the treatment once symptomatic severe stenosis develops?
nodes.a: Aortic valve replacement (surgical, or transcatheter in suitable patients)
nodes.note: Follow the aorta with periodic imaging. The ascending aorta is replaced at 5.5 cm (5.0 cm with risk factors), or at 4.5 cm or more when the valve is being replaced anyway.

nodes.q: His abnormal valve and murmur could suggest infective endocarditis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever + positive blood cultures + vegetations on the valve**; new regurgitant murmur
**No fever, negative cultures, calcified two-cusp valve with a click**

nodes.q: A calcified aortic valve could be postinflammatory (rheumatic) valve stenosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **History of rheumatic fever + fusion of the commissures of a three-cusp valve + mitral valve involvement**; no click
**Two cusps (single closure line) + ejection click + normal mitral valve + dilated ascending aorta**

nodes.note: The trap: both end in a calcified stenotic aortic valve.

nodes.q: A systolic click could suggest myxomatous degeneration. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur at the apex, louder on standing**; floppy thickened leaflets, Marfan syndrome
**Early ejection click at the base with stenosis murmur radiating to the neck**

root.stem: A 64-year-old man has painful purple toes on both feet 3 weeks after a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery. The pulses at his ankles and feet can be felt, and a net-like blotchy purple pattern covers both calves. His blood creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 2.9 mg/dL, and the eosinophil count is raised. He has no fever, his blood cultures are negative, and his leg is warm and not swollen.
root.oneliner: 64M + painful purple toes 3 weeks after femoral catheterization + palpable pedal pulses + net-like purple mottling of the calves + creatinine 1.0 to 2.9 + eosinophilia + no fever, negative blood cultures + warm, non-swollen legs
highlight: painful purple toes on both feet
pulses at his ankles and feet can be felt
creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 2.9 mg/dL

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Showers of cholesterol crystals from an aortic plaque lodge in small arteries. The clincher: **purple, painful toes with palpable pulses and a rising creatinine after aortic manipulation**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Livedo reticularis, the net-like pattern, is part of the picture.

nodes.q: Where do the emboli come from?
nodes.a: An ulcerated atherosclerotic plaque in the aorta that is broken up
nodes.note: Catheters, aortic surgery or clamping, and anticoagulants or thrombolytics can dislodge it.

nodes.q: Why are his pedal pulses still palpable?
nodes.a: The emboli block small arteries and arterioles, not the large arteries
nodes.note: Distal skin and muscle become ischemic while the main vessels remain open.

nodes.q: What does a biopsy show?
nodes.a: Needle-shaped (biconvex) clefts in small arteries, where cholesterol crystals dissolved during processing
nodes.note: A foreign-body giant cell reaction follows with intimal thickening and later occlusion.

nodes.q: Which organ failure explains his rising creatinine?
nodes.note: Often subacute over weeks, with eosinophilia and sometimes eosinophiluria and low complement. Other organs hit: gut (ischemia, pancreatitis), brain, retina.

nodes.q: Which drug class is added to stabilize the aortic plaque?
nodes.note: Treatment is supportive. Avoid further catheterization and stop anticoagulants or thrombolytics if possible; control blood pressure and give dialysis if needed. There is no thrombus to dissolve.

nodes.q: Dusky toes could be arterial thromboembolism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sudden pale, cold, painful, pulseless limb from a large-vessel clot** (atrial fibrillation or ventricular thrombus); affects one limb
**Palpable pulses + patchy purple toes + livedo reticularis + kidney injury**; often both feet

nodes.note: The trap: both follow arterial disease and cause ischemic toes; pulses separate them.

nodes.q: Purple toes could be septic emboli. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever + positive blood cultures + valve vegetations + Janeway lesions**
**No fever, negative cultures, after catheterization; eosinophilia**

nodes.q: Painful discolored legs could suggest venous thrombosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Swollen, warm, tender leg with normal toes; engorged superficial veins**
**Purple toes with no swelling and a net-like skin pattern**

nodes.q: Cold painful toes could be vasospasm. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Episodes of white, blue and red color change triggered by cold or stress that resolve**; fingers more than toes
**Persistent purple toes after aortic instrumentation + kidney injury**
